title: Kirkpatrick and Selman's 3-SAT finite-size scaling, re-measured: the exponent and 50% law replicate; the fitted threshold depends on the N range and instance model
abstract:
Kirkpatrick and Selman (KS; Science 264:1297, 1994) fitted the random 3-SAT satisfiability transition for N = 12 to 100 variables with finite-size scaling, $y = N^{1/
u}(\alpha-\alpha_c)/\alpha_c$, and reported $\alpha_c = 4.17 \pm 0.05$, $
u = 1.5 \pm 0.1$ (ranges of acceptable fits, judged by eye) and the 50% law $\alpha_{50} \approx 4.17 + 3.1N^{-2/3}$. We re-measured the transition with a complete modern solver and tested four pre-registered predictions. Method: 82,800 random 3-CNF formulas (3 distinct variables per clause, random signs, clauses drawn independently so duplicates are possible), each decided exactly by MiniSat 2.2 via python-sat; N in {12, 20, 24, 40, 50, 100} with $\alpha$ = 3.0 to 6.0 in steps of 0.1 and 400 formulas per point, plus N = 150 and 200 with $\alpha$ = 3.8 to 4.8 in steps of 0.05 and 200 per point. KS do not say whether they excluded duplicate clauses, so after review we repeated everything on a second set of 82,800 formulas without duplicate clauses. Per-N logistic fits give $\alpha_{50}(N)$ and the 10-90% width; a four-parameter collapse (logistic in y) is fitted by maximum likelihood. The collapse fits poorly (dispersion 3.3 to 3.4 on N up to 100), so collapse intervals are overdispersion-corrected profile intervals; others are 95% parametric bootstrap. Figures are given as (duplicates allowed / no duplicates). Results. (1) On KS's N range the collapse gives $
u$ = 1.52 / 1.52, interval [1.44, 1.62] in both, replicating KS's exponent. (2) It gives $\alpha_c$ = 4.08 [4.04, 4.11] / 4.12 [4.08, 4.14]. The point value 4.17 lies outside both intervals (corrected deviance 29.6 / 10.7; raw 101 / 35), and KS's published triple ($\alpha_c$ 4.17, $
u$ 1.5, $y_{50}$ 0.74) fits 88 / 30 corrected deviance units worse than the best collapse. But only the first interval lies wholly below KS's stated range 4.12 to 4.22: whether their range is excluded depends on the instance model, so we do not claim a refutation. (3) The fitted $\alpha_c$ moves with the N range: on N = 50 to 200 it is 4.20 [4.18, 4.22] / 4.19 [4.17, 4.21], above both N up to 100 intervals, against our pre-registered prediction that it would exceed 4.22. (4) KS's 50% law, extrapolated beyond their data, predicts the measured 50% points at N = 150 and 200 within 0.015 under both models: 4.292 / 4.282 against 4.280, and 4.271 / 4.269 against 4.261. It misses at the smallest size (N = 12: 4.935 / 4.859 against 4.761). (5) The 10-90% width at N = 50 to 200 gives an effective exponent $
u_{eff}$ = 1.42 [1.34, 1.51] / 1.46, below Wilson's asymptotic lower bound $
u \ge 2$, so the sharpening at these sizes is pre-asymptotic. Conclusion: KS's exponent and 50% law hold up, including out of sample; their $\alpha_c$ = 4.17 is best read as an effective, range- and procedure-dependent fitting parameter rather than an estimate of the threshold. Limitations: collapse results depend on the logistic scaling function and likelihood weighting ($\alpha_c$ trades off against $y_{50}$), and the model misfit makes all collapse intervals approximate; interval endpoints are resolved to a 0.01 grid; N is capped at 200; one solver. The duplicate-free arm, the convergence, misfit and profile analyses were added after pre-registration and are exploratory; predictions P1 to P4 and fits A1 to A5 were pre-registered, and P1 (on $\alpha_c$) and P2 were falsified as stated.

claims.text: On fresh random 3-SAT data at N = 12 to 100, a maximum-likelihood logistic finite-size-scaling collapse gives $\nu = 1.52$ (overdispersion-corrected 95% interval 1.44 to 1.62) with or without duplicate clauses, consistent with Kirkpatrick and Selman's $\nu = 1.5 \pm 0.1$.

For random 3-SAT at N = 12 to 100, $\alpha_c = 4.17$ lies outside the overdispersion-corrected 95% profile interval of a maximum-likelihood logistic collapse: 4.04 to 4.11 with duplicate clauses allowed, 4.08 to 4.14 without.

The collapse-fitted $\alpha_c$ for random 3-SAT rises with the N range: 4.08 (duplicates allowed) or 4.12 (none) on N = 12 to 100, versus 4.20 or 4.19 (corrected 95% intervals 4.18 to 4.22, 4.17 to 4.21) on N = 50 to 200.
Kirkpatrick and Selman's law $\alpha_{50} = 4.17 + 3.1N^{-2/3}$ predicts the measured random 3-SAT 50% points at N = 150 and N = 200 to within 0.015, with or without duplicate clauses.

For random 3-SAT at N = 50 to 200 the 10-90% transition width scales as $N^{-1/
u_{eff}}$ with $
u_{eff} = 1.42$ (95% CI 1.34 to 1.51; 1.46 without duplicate clauses), below the asymptotic bound $
u \ge 2$.

builds_on.note: Tested Table 1 (k = 3) nu = 1.5 +/- 0.1, alpha_c = 4.17 +/- 0.05, and the law alpha_50 = 4.17 + 3.1 N^(-2/3). nu replicates (1.52); the law predicts N = 150, 200 within 0.015; alpha_c = 4.17 is not recovered as a point estimate (4.08 or 4.12 by instance model), but their range is excluded only with duplicate clauses allowed.
